justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three time horizons, which is a common baseline assumption when there is no strong directional signal present. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 62.1 is anchored heavily to the current price or level, with very little expected movement given that short-term mean reversion and inertia tend to dominate over such a brief window. The one-week estimate of 62.3 drifts slightly higher, incorporating a small positive trend component that might reflect broader market momentum or a mild fundamental tailwind. The one-month estimate of 62.8 extends that drift further, assuming conditions remain relatively stable and that any underlying upward pressure accumulates gradually over time.

The confidence intervals widen appropriately as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 1.6 units wide captures primarily overnight and intraday volatility, which tends to be relatively contained. By one week, the interval expands to about 5.6 units, incorporating the possibility of new information arrivals, macro data releases, or sentiment shifts that could meaningfully move the level. At one month, the interval of about 10.7 units wide acknowledges that a great deal can change over four weeks, including policy decisions, earnings cycles, or geopolitical developments that were not foreseeable at the time of the forecast.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst such as a major policy announcement, a stronger-than-expected economic report, or a significant shift in investor sentiment could drive the level substantially above 68.2 within a month. On the downside, a risk-off event, an unexpected deterioration in fundamentals, or a liquidity shock could push the level well below 57.5. My intervals implicitly assume a relatively calm environment without fat-tail shocks, which is a limitation of any symmetric, normally-distributed confidence framework.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my estimates carry model uncertainty on top of the market uncertainty already embedded in the intervals. If the underlying data-generating process has shifted structurally, or if I am working from a stale or incomplete information set, my point estimates themselves could be systematically biased in one direction. The true probability of outcomes outside my stated 90% intervals may therefore be somewhat higher than the implied 10%, particularly at the one-month horizon where structural breaks have more time to materialize.
